rules.summary: `rel="canonical"` must be an absolute, fully-qualified URL
rules.why: Consumers read the literal attribute value, not the browser-resolved URL. A relative canonical means every consumer resolves it against whatever base it assumes — including the wrong origin.

rules.summary: Declare a `<link rel="canonical">` so search engines pick the right URL
rules.why: Without a canonical, engines choose among duplicate URLs (tracking params, http/https, trailing slashes) themselves — and may split ranking signals across them.

fix.title: Declare the canonical URL

rules.summary: The meta description summarizes this page truthfully
rules.why: The description is the one sentence you get to write in a search result. A boilerplate line repeated site-wide, or one that promises something the page does not deliver, gets replaced by improvised page text — or gets the click and loses the visitor.
rules.prose: Does the description accurately summarize this page's content, and is it written for this page rather than copied across the site?

rules.summary: Keep descriptions between 50 and 160 characters
rules.why: Snippets truncate around 160 characters and very short descriptions get replaced by improvised page text. Display folklore, not spec.

rules.summary: Provide a `<meta name="description">` on every indexable page
rules.why: The description feeds the search-result snippet. Without one, engines improvise from page text — usually worse than a sentence you wrote.

fix.title: Add a meta description

rules.summary: Every locale the sitemap publishes must appear in the route's `hreflang` cluster
Pages on a multilingual site must advertise their locale alternates
`<head>` alternates advertise a locale the sitemap does not list
rules.why: The two are derived from one intent by different code paths, so a disagreement means one of them is wrong. No specification says which: the declaration methods are equivalent, and a page can legitimately be cross-linked and kept out of the sitemap.
rules.prose: Your `<head>` advertises a translation your sitemap does not list. Is the sitemap missing an entry, or is the alternate pointing at a page you did not mean to publish?

rules.summary: Declare an `apple-touch-icon` for the iOS home screen
rules.why: iOS does not read `rel="icon"` for a home-screen shortcut. With no `apple-touch-icon` it screenshots the page instead, so what someone saved is a thumbnail of whatever was on screen when they saved it.

rules.summary: Serve a `/favicon.ico` at the root for the clients that ask blind
The manifest and the `<head>` must not disagree about the same icon
rules.why: Two files declare the icons, maintained by different hands, and nothing compares them. The failure worth naming is not that the two lists differ — they legitimately do, since an apple-touch-icon is not a manifest icon — but that they describe the *same file* differently, or that the icons exist only in the manifest, where a browser tab never looks.
rules.expected: the same size and type wherever an icon is declared twice

rules.summary: Declare an icon — the tab, the bookmark and the share sheet all read one
rules.why: No specification requires an icon, which is exactly why nothing complains and every consumer improvises. A browser falls back to `/favicon.ico` at the root, a feed reader or a link unfurler often falls back to nothing, and a bookmark to a site with no icon is a grey square among fifty.
rules.expected: at least one `<link rel="icon">`, or icons declared by a manifest

fix.title: Let the file convention declare it

rules.summary: A `sizes` attribute must describe the file it points at
rules.why: `sizes` is how a client picks one icon out of several without fetching them all, so a wrong value costs exactly what the attribute was there to save: the client downloads the file it was told to prefer and gets the wrong resolution. A half-true declaration is the common shape — a `.ico` carrying 16, 32 and 48 declared as `48x48` advertises one third of itself.
rules.expected: `sizes` listing what the file actually contains

rules.summary: A declared icon has to answer with an image
rules.why: An icon that 404s is worse than one never declared: the client asks, gets nothing, and has already skipped the `/favicon.ico` it would have fallen back to. The declaration is what took the fallback away.
rules.expected: a 2xx image at every declared icon URL

rules.summary: The declared `lang` is the language the page is actually written in
rules.why: A wrong `lang` is worse than a missing one: screen readers switch to the wrong pronunciation rules, browsers offer to translate a page that is already in the reader's language, and search engines file the page under the wrong audience. Nothing in the markup contradicts it, so no mechanical check can catch it.
rules.prose: Is the text of this page actually written in the language its `lang` attribute declares?

rules.summary: Set an explicit `og:description` for richer link unfurls
rules.why: A page that opted into Open Graph but omitted og:description gets unfurls that fall back to the meta description — or to nothing.

rules.summary: `og:image` must be an absolute URL
rules.why: Unlike a browser, the crawler that builds the preview has no document to resolve a relative path against — it reads the tag, not the page. A relative `og:image` is therefore not a smaller mistake than a missing one: the unfurl is identical, and the tag makes it look handled.

fix.title: Give Next a metadataBase, or write the origin in

rules.summary: Describe the shared image with `og:image:alt`
rules.why: The protocol defines `og:image:alt` as a description of what is in the image, and a generated card usually carries the page's title as pixels. Omitting it leaves that text sighted-only, in the one place a link is seen before anybody has opened the page. Optional in the vocabulary, which is why this is a guideline and not a spec violation.

fix.title: Carry the alt per image, not as a constant

rules.summary: Declare `og:image:width` and `og:image:height`
rules.why: A crawler that does not know the size cannot lay the card out until it has fetched the image, so the first share of a URL renders without it — the one share that matters most. The dimensions are the fix, and they cost two tags.

fix.title: Declare the size alongside the URL

rules.summary: Provide at least one `og:image` so links unfurl with a preview
rules.why: og:image is one of the four required Open Graph properties, and the one with the most visible payoff: without it, unfurls are text-only or pick a random body image.

fix.title: Add an og:image

rules.summary: Keep the shared image near the 1.91:1 the card is laid out for
rules.why: Meta's recommended 1200×630 is a shape before it is a size. An image far from it is not rejected — it is cropped to fit, and the crop is chosen by the consumer rather than by you.
rules.expected: a width ÷ height between 1.7 and 2.1 (1.91:1 is 1.9)

rules.summary: The URL in `og:image` has to answer with an image
rules.why: Every other check on a preview image judges the tag. This one judges the file, and it is the only one that can catch the failure with no symptom: a URL that is present, well-formed, absolute — and dead. The card renders empty and nothing in the page says why. Found on this project's own documentation, where eleven pages pointed at a route a redirect had been swallowing since the day it was written.

rules.summary: The `og:image` represents this page and survives the unfurl crop
rules.why: The preview image is the whole payload of a shared link. A generic site-wide banner, or artwork whose subject sits outside the ~1.91:1 crop, is present enough to pass every mechanical check and still communicate nothing.
rules.prose: Does the og:image represent what this page is about, rather than being a site-wide default, and does its subject survive being cropped to the 1.91:1 aspect ratio consumers render?

rules.summary: `og:image:width` and `og:image:height` must be the image's real size
rules.why:
The declared size is what a crawler lays the card out with before it has the file, which is the whole reason `og.image.dimensions` asks for it. A wrong one is therefore worse than none: the crawler reserves a shape the image does not have, and the card is letterboxed or cropped on the first share — the one that matters most.

It is also the declaration that blinds every other check. `og.image.ratio` reads these two numbers and refuses to fetch, so an invented 1200×630 scores 1.9 and passes over an image that is square. Found on a site whose cover art is 1024×1024 and one of whose covers is a 337-byte 1×1 placeholder, all three declared 1200×630 by a library that had never looked at them.
rules.expected: declared dimensions equal to the file's own

fix.title: Measure the image, or let the file convention do it

rules.summary: `og:locale:alternate` and the hreflang cluster must name the same locales
rules.why: Two vocabularies describe the same fact — this page exists in these languages — and nothing in a build keeps them in step, so they drift silently. Whichever one is short is the one telling a consumer that a translation it could have linked to does not exist.
rules.expected: one `og:locale:alternate` per hreflang locale other than this page's own

fix.title: Derive both lists from the same cluster

rules.summary: A translated page has to say which locale it is in
rules.why: `og:locale` defaults to `en_US` in the protocol itself — so a page that omits it does not decline to answer, it answers wrongly. On a site whose whole point is that the same page exists in several languages, every translation claims to be American English.
rules.expected: an `og:locale` on any page that declares hreflang alternates

fix.title: Emit the locale in the page's own metadata

rules.summary: Set an explicit `og:title` instead of relying on `<title>` fallback
rules.why: og:title is one of the four properties the Open Graph protocol requires. Consumers that fall back to `<title>` drag site-name boilerplate into the unfurl.

rules.summary: A page asking to be indexed must not be disallowed by robots.txt
`robots.txt` must not forbid crawling a site that asks to be indexed
`robots`, `googlebot`, and `X-Robots-Tag` must not contradict each other
rules.why: When directives conflict, crawlers resolve them with the most restrictive interpretation — a stray `noindex` wins over the `index` you meant, and the page silently drops out of search.
rules.expected: consistent indexing directives across meta tags and headers

rules.summary: `/robots.txt` should not redirect to another origin
Every line of robots.txt should parse as something
Rules past 500 KiB of robots.txt are not guaranteed to be read
A `Sitemap:` declaration must be an absolute URL
Non-standard robots.txt directives are read by some crawlers and ignored by others
A robots.txt that errors is read as forbidding the whole site
A sitemap that parses should list something
A sitemap must not list URLs that robots.txt forbids fetching
A sitemap should only list URLs on its own host
Every `<loc>` must be an absolute, parseable URL
A sitemap must not list URLs that ask not to be indexed
A sitemap should list canonical URLs
A sitemap may only list URLs under its own directory
A sitemap should not mix `http` and `https` entries
A sitemap should list final URLs, not URLs that redirect
Every URL a sitemap lists must answer
`<changefreq>` and `<priority>` must hold the values the protocol defines
Every child of a sitemap index must be reachable and parseable
`<lastmod>` must be a W3C Datetime, and must not be in the future
No single sitemap document may exceed 50,000 entries or 50 MB
A site should publish a sitemap
Indexable pages the crawl found should be listed in the sitemap
A located sitemap must be a well-formed `<urlset>` or `<sitemapindex>`
The `<title>` describes this specific page
rules.why: A title that repeats the site name, or describes the section rather than the page, gives a searcher no way to tell two results apart — and gives Google a reason to rewrite it into something you did not choose.
rules.prose: Does the title describe what is on THIS page specifically — not the site, not the section — and would it be distinguishable from the other pages of this site in a list of search results?

rules.summary: Keep `<title>` between 10 and 60 characters
rules.why: Long titles get truncated in search results and short ones waste the one line every result gets. The window is display folklore, not spec — Google states title length is not a ranking factor.

rules.summary: Every page needs a non-empty `<title>`
rules.why: The title element is required by the HTML standard and is the primary label search engines, browser tabs, bookmarks, and screen readers use for the page.

fix.title: Add a <title> to <head>
fix.snippet:
// app/…/page.tsx — App Router owns the <head>; never hand-write the tag.
export const metadata = { title: "Page name — Site name" };

rules.summary: Declare a `<meta name="viewport">` so mobile browsers render at the right scale
rules.why: Without a viewport declaration mobile browsers render at desktop width and scale down — unreadable text and a mobile-usability demotion.

fix.title: Add a viewport meta
fix.snippet:
// app/layout.tsx — a dedicated export, not part of `metadata`.
export const viewport = { width: "device-width", initialScale: 1 };
